title: PostgreSQL
summary: How it works under the hood and how to run it well.
why: Production databases fail in ways no prompt anticipates: bloat, locks, exhausted connections. Knowing how Postgres works inside lets you diagnose instead of guess.

cards.question: What does ACID mean?
cards.answer: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere) and Durability (committed data survives a crash).

cards.question: What is MVCC in PostgreSQL?
cards.answer: Each UPDATE creates a new row version and transactions see the one matching their snapshot. Readers do not block writers. Dead versions are cleaned up by VACUUM.

cards.question: How do you diagnose a slow query?
cards.answer: With EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS): it shows the real plan, timings, and estimated vs actual rows. A big gap between them usually means stale statistics (ANALYZE) or a missing index.

cards.question: Which index types does PostgreSQL offer and when to use each?
cards.answer: B-tree (default: equality and ranges), GIN (jsonb, arrays, full-text), GiST (geometry and ranges), BRIN (huge tables whose data correlates with physical order) and Hash (equality only).

cards.question: Why do you need connection pooling?
cards.answer: Each connection is a server process with a memory cost. Thousands of direct connections degrade the database. A pooler such as PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections over few real ones.

cards.question: How do you build a job queue on PostgreSQL?
cards.answer: With SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: each worker claims pending rows nobody else has locked, without waiting or double-processing. Fine for moderate volumes before moving to a dedicated broker.
